reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Bailey & Love (paediatric surgery)
clinicalPearls: A full-thickness abdominal wall defect, almost always to the right of the umbilical cord, through which bowel eviscerates without any covering membrane
Because the exposed bowel has no protective sac, it is vulnerable to fluid and heat loss and to inflammatory damage from amniotic fluid, so immediate protection is essential
Associated anomalies are uncommon apart from intestinal problems such as atresia, in contrast to omphalocele where extraintestinal anomalies are frequent
Immediate care centres on wrapping the exposed viscera in clear protective covering, maintaining warmth, aggressive fluid replacement, and gastric decompression
The infant should be nursed to avoid kinking of the mesentery, since the narrow defect can compromise blood flow to the herniated bowel
Closure may be achieved primarily if the defect and bowel volume allow, or staged using a silo to gradually reduce the bowel before fascial closure
Prolonged ileus and delayed feeding tolerance are expected postoperatively because of the intrauterine inflammatory thickening (peel) on the bowel
Most cases are detected antenatally on ultrasound and by a raised maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein, allowing planned delivery at a surgical centre
reference.pathophysiology: Gastroschisis is a defect in the anterior abdominal wall adjacent to the umbilicus, thought to result from a vascular or developmental disruption of the wall, allowing loops of bowel and occasionally other viscera to herniate freely into the amniotic cavity. Unlike omphalocele there is no covering sac, so the exposed intestine is bathed in amniotic fluid, becoming oedematous, foreshortened, and matted with an inflammatory peel. The small mesenteric opening also predisposes the herniated segment to ischaemia and to associated intestinal atresia.
additionalDifferentials: Body stalk anomaly / limb-body wall complex
additionalInvestigations: Antenatal ultrasound to confirm the diagnosis and monitor bowel appearance
Postnatal assessment of bowel viability and search for associated atresia
Serial electrolytes and fluid balance monitoring given large insensible losses
Echocardiography if any additional anomaly is suspected
redFlags: Exposed uncovered bowel requiring immediate protection to prevent catastrophic heat, fluid, and evaporative losses
Dusky, ischaemic, or constricted bowel at the defect indicating threatened viability and need for urgent intervention
Signs of hypovolaemia or hypothermia from inadequate resuscitation
Evidence of associated intestinal atresia or perforation requiring surgical planning
reference.prognosis: Survival is generally high with modern neonatal and surgical care. Recovery is often prolonged by intestinal dysmotility and delayed feeding, and outcome is worse when there is complex disease with atresia, perforation, or extensive bowel loss leading to short bowel syndrome.
pitfalls: Delaying protection of the exposed bowel, leading to hypothermia and severe fluid loss
Positioning the infant so the mesentery kinks and the bowel becomes ischaemic
Forcing primary closure under excessive tension and causing abdominal compartment syndrome
Underestimating the duration of postoperative ileus and stopping nutritional support too early
references: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
management: Immediate protection of the eviscerated bowel in a clear covering or bowel bag to limit heat, fluid and evaporative losses and allow inspection
Aggressive intravenous fluid resuscitation to replace large insensible losses, with nasogastric decompression to reduce bowel distension
Position and support the herniated viscera to prevent kinking of the narrow mesenteric pedicle and consequent ischaemia
Surgical closure by primary reduction and fascial repair where bowel volume allows, or staged reduction using a preformed silo before delayed closure
Parenteral nutrition to sustain the infant until intestinal dysmotility resolves and enteral feeding is established
Monitor for associated intestinal atresia, perforation, necrotising enterocolitis and short bowel syndrome
Manage within a neonatal intensive care and paediatric surgical multidisciplinary team, with antenatal counselling and planned delivery at a surgical centre
